newsitem.title: Japan: Japan firms cheer up some, credit still seen easy.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms cheer up some, credit still seen easy.

text.p: Japan's corporations grew somewhat cheerier about business prospects this month but are still wary about the future, according to a closely watched Bank of Japan survey released on Wednesday.

Economists said the data in the central bank's quarterly corporate survey, known as the "tankan" and seen as a key clue to monetary policy, confirmed their view that the central bank would keep its ultra-easy credit policy on hold well into 1997.
The tankan's diffusion index for big manufacturers -- an important gauge of corporate sentiment -- rose to minus three in November from minus seven in August, when the previous survey was conducted.
The figure was in line with private economists' forecasts, but below the zero predicted by the firms themselves in August.
The tankan also said that big manufacturers' diffusion index would rise only to minus one in March. The figure has not been in positive territory since November 1991.
The index represents the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those who expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.

Masayuki Matsushima, director of the BOJ's research and statistics department, said the tankan data showed that Japan's economy was improving gradually but steadily, with no signs of stalling. "Looking at the decisive factors for making judgments, the economy is gradually recovering," he told reporters. "It is gradual but firm."
But Matsushima also acknowledged that the recovery was not yet gaining strength and might lose speed, though temporarily.

Major non-manufacturing companies also grew more optimistic about their short-term prospects, with their diffusion index improving to zero from minus four in August. But the survey predicted their index would slip back to minus one in March.

Major companies said they expected their capital spending to rise seven percent in the 1996/97 business year, ending next March. That compared with their previous forecast of a 6.6 percent rise and an actual 1.2 percent rise the previous year.

Big manufacturers said they expected a 14.1 percent rise in profits in 1996/97, down from a 35.8 percent rise the previous year, while their non-manufacturing colleagues forecast an 8.1 percent rise against 16.4 percent growth in 1995/96.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, speaking in Osaka, said that while concerns remained, the tankan data showed the economy was firming up. "The tempo is gradual, but the economy is continuing to recover," he told a news conference.

Economists said the modest improvement in corporate sentiment -- which also included smaller firms -- would not prompt the Bank of Japan to tighten credit. Interest rates have been at rock-bottom levels since September 1995, when the BOJ slashed its official discount rate to a record low 0.5 percent.
A government source said recently that the BOJ and the Finance Ministry were growing more bullish about the economy, but their optimism was not yet backed by hard data.
"No policy change is to be expected, even though the BOJ is trying to say something positive," said Naofumi Kinoshita, a vice president at U.S. bank First Chicago in Tokyo.
Others echoed that view. "I think everything is fine until next March -- that is when I have problems, said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston in Tokyo.

Japan is set to raise its consumption tax to five percent from three percent on April 1. That, along with a possible end to special income tax cuts implemented for the past two years to keep the economic recovery on track, could drag growth down.
"Policy will remain unchanged...not because of the real economy per se, but because of financial sector weakness," Sasaki-Smith said.

Big Japanese banks have mostly finished dealing with the heavy load of bad loans inherited from the bursting of Japan's late 1980s "bubble" of soaring land and share prices. But smaller institutions still face problems, as evidenced by last week's failure of a second-tier regional bank, Hanwa Bank Ltd.

Japanese government bond cash and futures contracts rose sharply and the yen fell against most other currencies on expectations of continued low interest rates. The dollar was at around 113.15 yen in late afternoon trade.
